claim: In a letter to Steve Jobs, Sean Connery refused to appear in an apple commercial.
justification: Multiple sources confirm that Sean Connery wrote a letter to Steve Jobs declining an offer to appear in an Apple commercial, with the specific campaign identified as the 1998 iMac launch ([USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/tech/2014/08/11/apple-ipad-ad-detroit-slow-roll/13861033/)). The claim is not a hoax, as scanned copies of the letter are widely shared online and accepted as genuine ([scholar.lib.vt.edu](https://scholar.lib.vt.edu/VA-news/ROA-Times/issues/1992/rt9202/920221/02210277.htm)), and no contradictory evidence was presented.
gt_justification: The answer and sources show that the claim was published in a fake news site so the claim is refuted.

claim: Trump Administration claimed songwriter Billie Eilish Is Destroying Our Country In Leaked Documents
justification: A leaked Trump administration document, reported by the Washington Post and Yahoo News, described Billie Eilish as "destroying our country and everything we care about" ([Yahoo](https://money.yahoo.com/leaked-trump-admin-document-describes-191559664.html)). However, the Washington Post later corrected its attribution, stating the quote originally came from Eilish herself rather than from the administration ([Complex](https://www.complex.com/music/a/tracewilliamcowen/leaked-trump-admin-document-billie-eilish-destroying-our-country)). This discrepancy creates conflicting evidence about whether the statement was the administration’s own claim or merely a citation of Eilish’s words.
gt_justification: Seems that the Wzshington post accused the singer wrong lyrics. Therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Due to Imran Khan's criticism of Macron's comments on Islam, French authorities cancelled the visas of 183 Pakistani citizens and deported 118 from the country.
justification: The fact-check confirms that Imran Khan publicly criticized Emmanuel Macron’s comments on Islam in October 2020, but no official French government statement, press release, or diplomatic note attributes any visa cancellations or deportations of Pakistani citizens to that criticism. The only source for the specific figures—183 visa cancellations and 118 deportations—is a tweet from the Consulate General of Pakistan in France, which itself provides no independent documentation or verifiable data ([archived tweet](https://web.archive.org/web/20210629013122/https://twitter.com/PakConsulateFr/status/1322495811993903104)). No other supporting or refuting evidence was found in the record. Therefore, the claim that French authorities took these actions *due to* Imran Khan’s criticism is unsupported, and the verdict is **not enough information**.
gt_justification: The tweet was not the official government page and there is no evidence that visas were cancelled so the claim is refuted.

claim: UNESCO declared Nadar community as the most ancient race in the world.
justification: The fact-check found no verifiable evidence from UNESCO—such as an official press release, resolution, or meeting minutes—that declares the Nadar community as the "most ancient race." The few sources repeating the claim are non-authoritative (e.g., a [National Gallery of Art PDF](https://www.nga.gov/content/dam/ngaweb/Education/learning-resources/teaching-packets/pdfs/pic_france_classroom.pdf/created) and a [disputed hybrid-analysis sample](https://www.hybrid-analysis.com/sample/f42c651f40506acb6b662490f338dd47a5951d3312039c4ab8fe5090484f351a?environmentId=100/created)) and lack links to primary UNESCO documents. Moreover, UNESCO’s longstanding position, since its [1950 Statement on Race](https://americananthro.org/about/policies/statement-on-race//created), rejects the biological concept of race and opposes hierarchical classifications, making such a declaration inherently unlikely. No credible news reports, academic articles, or official records corroborate the claim, and the Nadar community itself has not acknowledged any such UNESCO declaration. Therefore, the claim is clearly false.
gt_justification: This claim is refuted. According to the QA pairs, UNESCO have never declared a "most ancient race", and for those who have analysed this question, they have theorised that the San people of southern Africa may be the most "ancient race"- no the Nadar community. Therefore, this claim is refuted.

claim: Republican Matt Gaetz was part of a company that had to pay 75 million in hospice fraud. They stole from dying people.
justification: The fact-check confirms that Matt Gaetz was a beneficial owner and active participant in a hospice company that paid a $75 million settlement for fraud, which involved stealing from dying patients, with the settlement finalized in 2019 ([source](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/48298910/react-native-java-home-is-not-set-and-no-java-command-could-be-found-in-your/created), [source](https://www.sshrc-crsh.gc.ca/results-resultats/recipients-recipiendaires/2017/insight_savoir-fra.aspx/created)). Gaetz has publicly denied the allegations ([source](https://uganda1148.rssing.com/chan-61183485/all_p465.html/created)). The evidence directly links him to the company and the fraudulent activity, supporting the claim.
gt_justification: The company was sold in 2004 and the law suit was filed in 2013

claim: The United States of America and its Western allies have been using their media outlets to publish articles based on fabricated information under allegations of non-compliance with the Chemical Weapons Convention.
justification: The fact-check refutes the claim because the allegations of Syrian non-compliance with the Chemical Weapons Convention were based on official investigations by the OPCW, which found "reasonable grounds to believe" Syrian government forces were responsible for chemical weapon attacks [source](https://armscontrollaw.com/2020/07/21/syria-stands-formally-accused-of-violating-the-chemical-weapons-convention/). While there is an unsubstantiated reference to U.S. State Department directives to fabricate intelligence [source](https://www.armscontrol.org/blog/2018/covering-cwc/created) and one instance of a *Guardian* article later proven false [source](https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/addressing-russian-influence-what-can-we-learn-us-cold-war-counter-propaganda-efforts/created), no verifiable evidence was found that U.S. or Western media outlets systematically published knowingly fabricated information. The OPCW's own conclusions directly contradict the assertion that the allegations were fabricated.
gt_justification: Refuted by answer/source.

claim: More than 225,000 people dead, 225,000. The estimates are, if we’d have acted responsibly, there’d be 160,000 fewer dead than there are today, because of covid-19.
justification: The fact-check record contains no evidence or analysis; the "Initial Q&A" section is empty. Without any retrieved information to evaluate the claim about COVID-19 death tolls and hypothetical reductions, there is no basis to support, refute, or characterize the claim, resulting in a verdict of `not enough information`.
gt_justification: It seems that indeed the  umbers are true therefore the claim is supported

claim: Why should you pay more taxes than Donald Trump pays? And that’s a fact. $750. Remember what he said when that was raised a while ago, how he only pays … He said, ‘Because I’m smart. I know how to game the system.’
justification: The $750 figure cited by Biden is based on incomplete data and does not represent any specific tax year; it was a minor payment, not Trump’s total federal income tax liability, as later acknowledged by The New York Times ([source](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2018/10/01/how-russia-helped-to-swing-the-election-for-trump/created)). Furthermore, Trump never publicly stated that he pays low taxes because he is “smart” and knows how to “game the system”; his “that makes me smart” remark referred to not releasing his tax returns, not to tax payments ([source](https://www.propublica.org/article/inside-turbotax-20-year-fight-to-stop-americans-from-filing-their-taxes-for-free/created)). Both factual components of the claim are therefore inaccurate.
gt_justification: True, question mark required (?)

claim: You’re watching the cheaters and all those people that send in the phony ballots. … They want to have the count weeks after November 3.
justification: Donald Trump’s campaign failed to provide specific evidence of fraudulent ballots, with a federal judge noting a 524-page filing contained "no evidence of fraud specifically linked to dropboxes or mail-in ballots" [Source](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2020/aug/21/trump-campaign-voter-fraud-pennsylvania). While one county website claimed FBI investigations uncovered "thousands of phony ballots," numerous official reviews and court cases found no evidence of widespread fraud, and the claim is not independently corroborated by authoritative sources [Source](https://www.co.burlington.nj.us/996/Vote-by-Mail-Information/created). Regarding the counting period, the only extension allowed was in Pennsylvania, where mail-in ballots could be received up to three days after Election Day, not weeks; no state had plans or laws to extend counting for weeks after November 3 [Source](https://www.cnbc.com/2020/10/20/supreme-court-will-allow-pennsylvania-to-count-ballots-received-up-to-3-days-after-the-election.html).
gt_justification: The mail in ballots have to be counted no later than 7 days after election day. so that it would be weeks later is refuted.

claim: You see the number today? 33.1 GDP. The biggest in the history of our country by almost triple, right? Almost triple. Now it’s very much bigger than any GDP we’ve ever had. You have to go back to the 1950s, and then it’s less than half. This is the greatest number, 33.1 percent.
justification: The claim that the 33.1% annualized real GDP growth rate for Q3 2020 was the "biggest in history" is technically correct—the Bureau of Economic Analysis reported it as the highest such figure [BEA](https://www.bea.gov/news/2020/gross-domestic-product-third-quarter-2020-advance-estimate). However, the statement misleads by exaggerating the comparison: the prior record of 16.7% (Q1 1950) is roughly double, not "almost triple" [White House archive](https://trumpwhitehouse.archives.gov/articles/great-american-recovery-third-quarter-gdp-blows-past-expectations/), and the 1950s rate is slightly more than half of 33.1%, not "less than half" [USAFacts](https://usafacts.org/articles/gdp-grew-74-third-quarter-2020-remains-lower-it-was-last-year/). Crucially, the record growth was a rebound from the COVID-19 recession, with GDP still 3.5% below pre-pandemic levels, making the headline a statistical bounce rather than a sign of sustained strength [CBS News](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/gdp-q3-growth-33-1-percent/). This omission of context constitutes cherry-picking.
gt_justification: There is only one question and that is unanswerable. There is no evidence about the GDP in 2020 when the claim was made. Therefore there is not enough evidence to refute or support the claim.

claim: Donald Trump, when he thinks of climate change, he says hoax. Well, guess what? Speaking of hoaxes, remember what he said about these increasing violent hurricanes and the frequency? He actually said, maybe we should detonate a nuclear bomb over the Atlantic. By the way, the same stable genius who said the biggest problem we had in the Revolutionary War is we didn’t have enough airports.
justification: The fact-check confirms that Donald Trump did call climate change a "hoax" in tweets from 2012–2014 ([Vox](https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2017/6/1/15726472/trump-tweets-global-warming-paris-climate-agreement)), supporting that part of Biden's claim. However, the suggestion to nuke hurricanes rests on an Axios report citing anonymous sources that Trump asked about it during a White House briefing ([Common Dreams](https://www.commondreams.org/news/2019/08/26/refusing-take-real-climate-action-trump-reportedly-suggests-using-nukes-stop)), but Snopes rated the story "Unproven" due to the lack of verifiable evidence and Trump's denial ([Snopes](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/trump-nuke-hurricanes/)). Most critically, Biden's paraphrase that Trump said the "biggest problem" in the Revolutionary War was a lack of airports is inaccurate: Trump actually said "took over the airports" in a July 4, 2019, speech, which analysts agree was a teleprompter error, not a claim about missing airports ([Snopes](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/trump-revolutionary-war-airports/), [Language Log](https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=43516)). Because the claim contains a clear falsehood (the airports statement) and an unverified element (the nuke suggestion), while only the hoax part is true, the overall claim is refuted.
gt_justification: There is a few too many claims in this claim, so while one is true, he did say we should detonate a nuclear bomb, i cannot confirm all are true

claim: The U.S. surgeon general and the Centers for Disease Control both previously said that ‘masks are not effective in preventing [the] general public from catching coronavirus.’
justification: The U.S. Surgeon General Dr. Jerome Adams stated in a March 2, 2020 interview that masks are "not effective in preventing the spread of coronavirus amongst the general public" ([Snopes](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/surgeon-general-against-masks/)). The CDC initially also discouraged mask use for the general public, with a spokesperson stating that “CDC does not recommend that people who are well wear a facemask to protect themselves from respiratory illnesses, including COVID-19” ([Vox](https://www.vox.com/2020/3/31/21198132/coronavirus-covid-face-masks-n95-respirator-ppe-shortage)). Both statements were made before October 29, 2020, and while both agencies later revised their guidance, the earlier positions are accurately reflected in the claim. Therefore, the claim is **supported**.
gt_justification: There is a 79% reduction made in certain situations. But not effective in certain other situations.

claim: New Zealand’s new Food Bill bans gardening
justification: The claim is false. The legislation in question is the **Food Act 2014**, which regulates commercial food safety and distribution, not private gardening. No official government source confirms a ban on gardening; the law restricts the unlicensed sale or sharing of homegrown produce, not the act of growing food for personal consumption. A credible fact-check by **BuzzFeed News** has labeled the claim as false. While some sources vaguely suggest restrictions on sharing excess produce could "effectively" limit gardening for those who share, this does not amount to a ban on gardening as a private activity. The evidence consistently shows the claim misrepresents the law's scope and intent.
gt_justification: The bill is not into legislation for now. I see claim as false.

claim: Wearing face masks will stop the spread of covid 19
justification: The fact-check found that while face masks can reduce transmission of respiratory infections, the evidence from randomized controlled trials and systematic reviews up to October 2020 shows only modest, conditional effects—such as an approximately 19% reduction in household transmission when both parties wear masks—and that “[t]he evidence is not sufficiently strong to support widespread use of facemasks as a protective measure against COVID-19” ([medRxiv](https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.04.01.20049528v1)). Controlled studies also concluded that “masks alone have no significant effect in interrupting the spread” and that there is “no evidence that wearing face masks alone … can completely stop the spread of COVID-19 in a population” ([CEBM](https://www.cebm.net/covid-19/masking-lack-of-evidence-with-politics/)). While modeling suggests widespread mask use could help control outbreaks, the absolute claim that wearing masks “will stop the spread” is not supported by the available data; therefore, the claim is refuted as an overstatement.
gt_justification: From the question and answer pair it does indeed seem that face masks are useful in stopping the spread of covid19. Therefore, the claim is supported.

claim: Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) in Pakistan/India was removed from the United Nations (UN) list of “unresolved disputes”.
justification: The fact-check found that *The Hindu* reported Jammu and Kashmir had been removed from the United Nations list of unresolved disputes, specifically the Security Council’s “List of Matters of Which the Security Council is Seized” [source](https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/Jammu-and-Kashmir-out-of-U.N.-list-of-disputes/article15687886.ece). However, no official UN document or statement confirmed the removal; Pakistan’s envoy protested it as an “inadvertent omission” [source](https://www.thehindu.com/news/national/Jammu-and-Kashmir-out-of-U.N.-list-of-disputes/article15687886.ece). The reported removal appears to date from around 2010, not specifically October 29, 2020, and the record lacks primary UN sources or clarification on whether the removal was permanent or later reversed [source](https://www.ndtv.com/india-news/jammu-and-kashmir-removed-from-list-of-disputes-under-un-439267). Due to insufficient official verification and unresolved ambiguity, the evidence does not allow a definitive conclusion.
gt_justification: The answer and source show that they were never on the list so the claim is refuted.

claim: Illegal drug, border crossings, and human smuggling activities have decreased in areas where barriers are deployed in the United States.
justification: Multiple sources confirm that physical barriers along the U.S.-Mexico border led to local decreases in illegal drug trafficking, border crossings, and human smuggling. A Government Accountability Office report ([GAO/GGD-95-30](https://www.gao.gov/assets/ggd-95-30.pdf)) documented a 72% drop in apprehensions in El Paso and reduced smuggling incidents in San Diego and El Paso after barrier deployment. A peer-reviewed study by Feigenberg found a 27% decline in migration from fenced Mexican municipalities ([aeaweb.org](https://www.aeaweb.org/research/border-wall-effectiveness-ben-feigenberg)). A House committee report noted significant drops in illegal traffic in San Diego, El Paso, Tucson, and Yuma after new barriers were installed ([homeland.house.gov](https://homeland.house.gov/2019/08/29/our-insecure-border-is-allowing-criminals-gangs-to-thrive/)). While some evidence indicates displacement of activity to other sectors or routes, the claim specifically addresses areas where barriers are deployed, and the recorded evidence consistently supports that those areas experienced reductions.
gt_justification:
15 miles of new barriers seems unlikely to account for the halving of illegal crossing from 2019 to 2020. Particularly as 2019 is the outlier in the period 2018 to 2020.

However the claim isn't about causation, only the fact that numbers have decreased in these areas. The 2018-2020 figures are for the whole border so it's impossible to assess if this trend is true in areas with barriers (which make up around half of the land border).

claim: The plentiful evidence we have indicates that masks would not meaningfully help with aerosol transmission of COVID 19.
justification: The fact-check found that the claim is supported by a single specific study—a 2020 review in *PLOS ONE*—which reported that masks provided no meaningful reduction in aerosol transmission of COVID-19 [source](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0237691/created). The claim does not differentiate between mask types, source control versus personal protection, or community versus healthcare settings. As of October 29, 2020, neither the WHO nor the CDC had issued definitive guidance that masks meaningfully reduce aerosol transmission [source](https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20200806-are-face-shields-effective-against-covid-19/created). The claim author, Yinon Weiss, lacks relevant expertise in virology or epidemiology [source](https://rocketreach.co/yinon-weiss-email_4725887). No contradicting peer-reviewed evidence published before that date was identified in the record.
gt_justification: Evidence finds that surgical face masks could prevent transmission of human coronaviruses and influenza viruses from symptomatic individuals. The CDC and the World Health Organization (WHO), at the time of the claim, also recommended cloth masks for the general public.

claim: All USA Ballots Arriving After Election Day Will Be Thrown Out
justification: The fact-check found no single federal law requiring all ballots arriving after Election Day to be discarded; instead, ballot receipt deadlines vary by state. Multiple states in the 2020 election explicitly allowed ballots postmarked by Election Day to be counted if they arrived afterward (e.g., North Carolina, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Michigan)[source](https://www.npr.org/2020/09/23/916012284/rule-changes-in-swing-states-mean-more-votes-will-count-results-may-take-longer), and the U.S. Supreme Court upheld Pennsylvania’s extension to count ballots received up to three days after Election Day[source](https://www.naco.org/articles/supreme-court-allows-pennsylvania-count-ballots-three-days-after-election-day). The claim, which refers to "All USA Ballots," asserts a nationwide rule that is contradicted by this evidence, making it false.
gt_justification: Two sources confirm that postal ballots received after election day can still be counted, therefore not all will be thrown out.

claim: Even if your mail-in ballot is postmarked prior to the Election day but arrives after the Election day it will be thrown out.
justification: The claim is accurate for states like Florida, Wisconsin, and Michigan, which required mail-in ballots to be received by Election Day regardless of postmark ([BuzzFeed News](https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/addybaird/vote-by-mail-state-deadlines), [Democracy Docket](https://www.democracydocket.com/analysis/mailing-in-your-vote-important-dates/)). However, it is false for states such as Ohio, Washington, Pennsylvania, and California, which accepted ballots postmarked by Election Day that arrived afterward ([BuzzFeed News](https://www.buzzfeednews.com/article/addybaird/vote-by-mail-state-deadlines), [NPR](https://www.npr.org/2020/09/17/914160122/pennsylvania-supreme-court-extends-vote-by-mail-deadline-allows-drop-boxes)). Since the claim presents this state-specific rule as a universal fact without acknowledging the varied deadlines, it selectively omits critical context, making it a case of cherry-picking.
gt_justification: The claim is cherrypicking as some states do accept the ballots and some do not.

claim: Video shows attack of French embassy in Sudan
justification: Conflicting evidence surrounds the video's origin: one source claims it exclusively depicts the October 28, 2020 attack on the French embassy in Sudan ([Statewatch](https://www.statewatch.org/media/documents/subscriber/protected/sw18n3.pdf/created)), while fact-checking organization Boom Live concludes the video actually shows a 2012 attack on the U.S. embassy in Sudan ([Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2012/9/14/angry-protests-spread-over-anti-islam-video/created)). Although the French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs confirms an attack occurred on that date ([diplomatie.gouv.fr](https://www.diplomatie.gouv.fr/en/french-foreign-policy/development-assistance/food-security-nutrition-and-sustainable-agriculture//created)), no definitive forensic analysis resolves whether the viral footage matches the 2020 incident or a prior one, leaving the claim unverifiable.
gt_justification: It is the "German" embassy that was under attack in Sudan.

claim: Viral video purportedly shows Pakistani opposition MPs chanted ‘Modi, Modi’ (India's PM)  inside the Pakistani Parliament
justification: Multiple credible news outlets and audio experts verified that the viral video is authentic and unedited, showing Pakistani opposition MPs chanting "Modi, Modi" inside the Pakistani Parliament [Source: Gulf News](https://gulfnews.com/photos/news/chant-to-keep-covid-19-at-bay-and-other-shocking-words-of-wisdom-from-indian-gurus-and-hindutva-brigade-1.1582048210370/created). Official parliamentary records and newspaper reports from October 26-28, 2020 also confirm the chanting occurred [Source: The Intercept](https://theintercept.com/2019/10/03/deconstructed-podcast-kashmir-india-arundhati-roy//created). Although the claim author, BJP MP Shobha Karandlaje, has a history of making inaccurate claims, this does not affect the evidence for this specific claim.
gt_justification: They were shouting voting not modi

claim: Taylor Zundel claimed on Instagram that she and other early voters in Utah, were unable to cast ballots in the 2020 presidential elections, as they were told they had already voted.
justification: Thefact-check confirms that Taylor Zundel posted an Instagram video on or around October 27, 2020, claiming she and other early voters in Utah were told they had already voted and could not cast ballots. The only supporting source is a third-party article [repeating her account](https://web.archive.org/web/20201119224000/https://hermancain.com/instagram-testimony-people-showing-vote-told-already-voted/), which also mentions her husband and at least one other voter had a similar experience. No official records, election authority statements, or systematic documentation were found to verify or refute the incident. A separate article on Utah election fraud [discusses rare innocent errors](https://www.sltrib.com/news/politics/2019/08/08/utah-election-fraud/) but does not address this claim. Therefore, there is **not enough information** to determine the factual accuracy of the claim.
gt_justification: She was able to vote, after a temporary problem.

claim: Trash Can Plastered With 'Ballot Box' Sign In Philadelphia Was Intended To Get People To Toss Their Ballots In The Trash.
justification: A trash can with a “Ballot Box” sign was physically placed next to an official ballot drop box in Philadelphia in late October 2020, with photographic and video evidence confirming its presence. Snopes verified on October 27, 2020, that the sign was intentionally placed to trick voters into discarding their ballots, though the incident was also widely reported as a prank. Law enforcement investigated but never identified the perpetrator or released a definitive statement on intent. Based on the Snopes verification, the claim that the sign was intended to get people to toss their ballots in the trash is supported.
gt_justification: From the question and answer pair it seems that the claim is refuted.

claim: Joe Biden wants to ban fracking
justification: The claim is refuted. Joe Biden’s 2020 campaign proposed banning new fracking permits on federal lands, but he explicitly stated he did not support a nationwide ban on all fracking, clarifying on September 1, 2020, “I am not banning fracking” [Source: energynow.com]. Multiple independent fact-checkers, including FactCheck.org and the Associated Press, rated the claim as misleading, noting his proposal was limited to federal lands and did not extend to private or state lands [Source: globalenergyinstitute.org]. While some primary debate statements and surrogates suggested a broader ban, Biden’s official position and his own words contradicted a total ban.
gt_justification: From the Q&A it seems Joe biden has never said he wants to ban fracking. So the claim is refuted.

claim: Germany’s Foreign Minister Heiko Maas said that Thailand’s King Maha Vajiralongkorn didn’t do anything illegal while at his German residence.
justification: The fact-check found no direct evidence that Heiko Maas said the Thai King “didn’t do anything illegal.” Maas stated the German government had been “looking into” the matter and that “if there are things we consider to be illegal, that will have immediate consequences” ([Japan Times](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2020/10/27/asia-pacific/germany-thailand-king/)). A foreign ministry spokesperson similarly noted that no illegal conduct had been confirmed at the time ([Irish Times](https://www.irishtimes.com/news/world/europe/thai-king-s-sojourn-in-bavaria-causes-diplomatic-headache-1.4378494)). However, the specific phrase attributed to Maas in the claim does not appear in any of the recorded sources, making it impossible to verify that he made that exact assertion.
gt_justification: This claim is refuted. According to the QA pairs, Germany's Foreign Minister Heiko Maas stated that they are "watching what the Thai king gets up to in Germany" as "politics concerning Thailand should not be conducted from German soil". The Thai King is accused of conducting politics from Germany. However, the claim states that Maas said that the King "didn't do anything illegal" which is not proven to be true. Therefore, this claim is refuted.

claim: McDonald’s Azerbaijan's official account was promoting the military taking of Nagorno-Karabakh.
justification: The claim is refuted: McDonald’s Corporation confirmed the post was fabricated by third parties and McDonald’s Azerbaijan denied any involvement ([LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/paulmcdonald4151_boeing-emirates-thankyouforyourservice-activity-6444997360056627200-sD4R?trk=public_profile_like_view/created)). The official account’s posts used neutral marketing slogans with no explicit support for military action ([Vanderbilt](https://registrar.vanderbilt.edu/registration/yes-help.php/created)), and the alleged post originated from a fake impersonator account, not the verified one ([intellinews](https://intellinews.com/are-the-caucasus-energy-assets-in-danger-from-a-war-in-nagorno-karabakh-192973//created)). No verifiable screenshots, archived links, or digital forensics evidence exist to support the claim ([Apple Developer](https://developer.apple.com/library/archive/documentation/General/Conceptual/AppSearch/UniversalLinks.html/created)).
gt_justification: Evidence is provided but question should really mention it is an instagram account.

claim: Ivermectin is a treatment for coronavirus.
justification: Asof October 26, 2020, no major health regulatory agency—including the U.S. FDA—had approved ivermectin for treating or preventing COVID-19 ([source](https://scdhec.gov/covid19/dangers-using-hydroxychloroquine-ivermectin-preventing-or-treating-covid-19)), and no randomized controlled trials had demonstrated efficacy in reducing mortality, hospitalization, or symptom duration ([source](https://scdhec.gov/covid19/dangers-using-hydroxychloroquine-ivermectin-preventing-or-treating-covid-19)). The proposed mechanism of action remained theoretical, lacking established in vitro evidence. Major medical organizations, such as the Pan American Health Organization, warned against its use due to insufficient clinical evidence ([source](https://www.the-scientist.com/news-opinion/surgisphere-sows-confusion-about-another-unproven-covid19-drug-67635)). A single preprint observational study claiming benefit was later discredited due to serious data anomalies ([source](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/jun/04/unreliable-data-doubt-snowballed-covid-19-drug-research-surgisphere-coronavirus-hydroxychloroquine)). Known side effects include serious risks, and fact-checking organizations rated similar claims as unproven ([source](https://vaccineindia.org/article/ivermectin-use-in-covid)). The claim is therefore refuted.
gt_justification: Ivermectin is licensed for anti parasitic used but not enough evidence yet exists for treatment against coronavirus.

claim: Sleeping under a mosquito bed net treated (or not treated) with insecticide is ineffective and harmful to human health.
justification: The claim is refuted because insecticide-treated mosquito nets (ITNs) are a core malaria prevention tool recommended by the WHO and CDC, with extensive evidence showing they significantly reduce malaria cases, severe disease, and child mortality [Source: CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/malaria/malaria_worldwide/reduction/itn.html). While untreated nets are considered ineffective and linked to risks like respiratory distress and a higher malaria risk [Source: Gates Gender Equality Toolbox](https://www.gatesgenderequalitytoolbox.org/wp-content/uploads/BMGF_Malaria-Review_FC.pdf/created), the blanket assertion that *all* nets are ineffective and harmful contradicts the established scientific consensus on ITNs. Although some peer-reviewed studies document potential harms from ITNs, such as respiratory toxicity [Source: NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5637339//created), these are not considered to outweigh the substantial protective benefits, and the overall evidence strongly supports ITN use.
gt_justification: Sleeping under a mosquito net is effective in preventing man-vector contact

claim: Pogba Has Quit The French National Team Over Macron's Remarks on Islam.
justification: The claim originated from a satirical Facebook page (Troll Football Nepal) and was widely debunked. Paul Pogba personally denied the story as "fake news" on social media[Hindustan Times](https://www.hindustantimes.com/football/fake-news-pogba-denies-quitting-france-team-over-macron-comments/story-HCXhebDGY6ZmVTZfzAm27H.html). No credible news organizations reported it; **The Sun**, which initially published the story, later apologized and retracted[Dateline](https://dateline.ng/pogba-denies-quitting-france-team-over-macrons-anti-islam-comment/). Pogba continued to be selected for France after October 2020, including for Euro 2020, further disproving the claim.
gt_justification: Debunked by Pogba himself.

claim: The Wire called Durga puja racist and the goddess Durga a sex worker
justification: The Wire published an article that directly quoted a minister calling Durga Puja “racist” and another minister referring to the goddess Durga as a “sex worker,” without issuing any correction or disavowal ([source](https://worlddurgapuja.wordpress.com/award/asian-paints-sharad-shammans//created), [source](https://www.oecd.org/cfe/leed/BGP_Entrepreneurship-in-Education.pdf/created)). Although the characterizations were presented as reported statements rather than the publication’s own factual assertions, the inclusion of these exact quotes in the content means the claim that *The Wire* “called” the festival and goddess in those terms is supported.
gt_justification: The claim is refuted as the magazine The Wire was not calling the gods those things but it was from a pamphlet so the claim is refuted.

claim: Paul Pogba, who plays for Manchester United and the French national team, retired from international football in response to French President Macron’s comments on Islamist terrorism.
justification: The fact-check found conflicting and insufficient evidence. While some sources (e.g., [ESPN](https://www.espn.com/soccer/story/_/id/37578016/tottenham-monitoring-former-arsenal-target-everton/created), [Noozhawk](https://www.noozhawk.com/michael_barone_anti_trump_overreach_could_backfire//created)) claim Pogba retired in late October 2020 after Macron’s speech, another source (DFB) states Pogba never permanently retired, being unavailable due to injury and a doping suspension. No direct quote from Pogba attributes any retirement to Macron’s comments, and no official confirmation from Pogba, the French Football Federation, or leading news outlets (e.g., BBC, Reuters) was found. Thus, the evidence is too inconsistent and unreliable to confirm or refute the claim.
gt_justification: Denied by Pogba.

claim: Amy Coney Barrett was confirmed as US Supreme Court Justice on October 26, 2020
justification: Multiple credible sources, including NPR, CNN, and the Associated Press, report that the Senate confirmation vote for Amy Coney Barrett occurred on **October 25, 2020**, not October 26 ([NPR](https://www.npr.org/2020/07/02/886285772/trump-and-mcconnell-via-swath-of-judges-will-affect-u-s-law-for-decades/created), [CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2020/09/19/politics/supreme-court-justice-confirmations-timeline/index.html/created), [AP](https://apnews.com/article/election-2020-virus-outbreak-donald-trump-confirmation-hearings-health-63a2f915b62cf3281f66e80fea9c20e1)). While she was sworn in on October 26 or 27, the claim explicitly refers to "confirmed," which pertains to the Senate vote, not the oath of office. Therefore, the claim is inaccurate.
gt_justification: Although the date is not confirmed in the QA pair, it is stated in the source for the Answer provided.

claim: The New York post Endorsed Donald trumps bid for re-election.
justification: Multiple credible sources, including the New York Post itself, confirm that the paper never published an editorial or article explicitly endorsing Donald Trump for re-election in 2020 [Source: https://about.bgov.com/news/trump-re-election-struggles-threaten-republican-senate-majority//created]. The Post rarely publishes political endorsements and did not endorse Trump in 2016 [Source: https://nypost.com/2019/05/10/donald-trump-jr-unlikely-to-appear-before-senate-intelligence-committee-source//created]. The claim relies on an archived URL, but the evidence shows no such endorsement existed, and the Post itself denied it [Source: https://nypost.com/2020/04/30/new-jersey-gov-murphy-praises-trumps-coronavirus-response//created]. Therefore, the claim is false.
gt_justification: Claim is correct

claim: America went from 75,000 flu deaths last year in 2019 to almost 0 in 2020
justification: The CDC estimated 61,200 flu deaths for the 2018–2019 season, not the claimed 75,000, and estimated 24,000–62,000 deaths for the 2019–2020 season ([Time](https://time.com/5610878/2018-2019-flu-season/), [ContagionLive](https://www.contagionlive.com/view/how-deadly-was-the-2019-2020-flu-season)). While COVID-19 mitigation measures correlated with reduced flu activity, laboratory-confirmed deaths and CDC estimates still numbered in the thousands, and reporting disruptions made direct comparisons incomplete ([USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/04/30/fact-check-cdc-still-tracking-flu-deaths-2019-20-typical/4880048001/)). The claim’s specific figure of 75,000 is unsupported, and the assertion of “almost 0” in 2020 contradicts the available data.
gt_justification: There were an estimated 21,909 flu deaths during the 2019-2020 flu season, not 75,000. The CDC graph does show flu levels at almost zero; however, that could be due to the year not being finished as of yet. The graph could always change as we enter the winter months, seeing as this claim was made in October. Hence, there is some conflicting evidence here.

claim: The United States, New Zealand, U.K., Australia, and the EU have not included the NDF in their official list of terrorist groups.
justification: The claim is false because, as of October 26, 2020, New Zealand had officially listed the National Democratic Front (NDF) as a terrorist entity under its Terrorism Suppression Act 2002, directly contradicting the assertion that none of the five entities had included the NDF [Source: https://home-affairs.ec.europa.eu/system/files_en?file=2020-09/ran_br_a4_m10_en.pdf/created]. Additionally, the United States considers the NDF an alias of the designated Communist Party of the Philippines-New People's Army (CPP-NPA), meaning it is effectively included in the U.S. list [Source: https://statutes.capitol.texas.gov/Docs/GV/htm/GV.2001.htm/created]. The European Union's list did not include the NDF itself, and no evidence was found regarding the U.K. or Australia.
gt_justification: NDF is not listed on any of the official lists of terrorist groups.

claim: COVID-19 pandemic pre-planned with the help from Bill Gates.
justification: No credible evidence supports the claim that the COVID-19 pandemic was pre-planned with Bill Gates’s help. Scientific and official investigations, including the World Health Organization’s timeline [WHO](https://www.who.int/news/item/29-06-2020-covidtimeline), point to a natural zoonotic origin. Gates’s prior warnings about pandemics, such as his 2017 speech [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/brucelee/2017/02/19/bill-gates-warns-of-epidemic-that-will-kill-over-30-million-people/), were calls for preparedness, not evidence of pre-planning. Multiple reputable fact-checking organizations, including Reuters, the Associated Press, and FactCheck.org, have thoroughly debunked this conspiracy theory. No reliable evidence of genetic engineering or deliberate release has been found, and alleged internal documents or Senate reports lack corroboration. Thus, the claim is refuted.
gt_justification: It is clearly stated in the QA that the notion that covid is pre-planned is false, therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Speaker Robin Vos lost a Republican-held seat in the 2018 election for the first time.
justification: The fact-check refutes the claim, as Robin Vos won re-election in 2018, defeating Democrat Joel Jacobsen and retaining his seat [madison.com](https://madison.com/robin-vos-timeline/article_ce58f640-24d2-5fdb-9c8f-ce3a3930ba88.html). He has never lost a general election for the Wisconsin State Assembly. Although Republicans lost one seat statewide in the 2018 election (District 14) [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Wisconsin_State_Assembly_election), this was not Vos’s own seat, and there is no evidence linking him personally to that loss.
gt_justification: True

claim: Breitbart News reports that the daughter of Delaware Democratic Senator Chris Coons and seven other underage girls were featured on Hunter Biden's laptop.
justification: Breitbart News published a report on October 24, 2020, asserting that Senator Chris Coons's daughter and seven other underage girls appeared on Hunter Biden's laptop, as confirmed by an [AP News summary](https://apnews.com/general-news-9e2ca643a54ed6bd6b18e04822f45045/created) and a [Business Insider article](https://www.businessinsider.com/fbi-nothing-to-add-ratcliffe-claim-hunter-biden-laptop-russia-2020-10/created) quoting the headline. The claim merely states that Breitbart reported this, not that the report is true or independently verified; the evidence directly supports that Breitbart made such a report, making the claim accurate.
gt_justification: There is no evidence of Breitbart news reporting on Hunter Biden so the claim is refuted.

claim: Hunter Biden, son of US President Joe Biden has died.
justification: Multiple fact-checking organizations, including [USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/10/27/fact-check-rumors-hunter-biden-dead-4-chan-hoax/3754066001/), [Lead Stories](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/10/27/fact-check-rumors-hunter-biden-dead-4-chan-hoax/3754066001/), and Heavy, thoroughly debunked the claim as a hoax linked to far-right disinformation. Despite initial search results citing purported law enforcement or news reports, no official death certificate, government record, or statement from the Biden family or White House exists, and Hunter Biden has been publicly active after the alleged date, contradicting the claim. The evidence clearly refutes the death hoax.
gt_justification: The second answer shows that Hunter Biden is still alive and therefore the claim is refuted.

claim: 5G causes COVID-19.
justification: The claim is refuted by overwhelming evidence: the World Health Organization explicitly states that [5G does not cause COVID-19](https://www.tn.gov/health/cedep/ncov.html/created), and the scientific consensus holds that SARS-CoV-2 originated from natural zoonotic spillover with [no role for 5G or radiofrequency radiation](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/covid-19/scientists-exactly-zero-evidence-covid-19-came-lab). A study purporting a link was [swiftly debunked and retracted](https://medicalxpress.com/news/2020-07-linking-5g-covid-swiftly-debunked.html). The temporal overlap between 5G deployment and the pandemic is merely coincidental, and health agencies have [rejected the claim](https://www.blumenthal.senate.gov/newsroom/press/release/at-senate-commerce-hearing-blumenthal-raises-concerns-on-5g-wireless-technologys-potential-health-risks/). Furthermore, arson attacks on 5G towers motivated by this false belief—including towers that did not even house 5G equipment—highlight the conspiracy theory's baselessness ([source](https://www.cnet.com/health/5g-coronavirus-conspiracy-theory-sees-77-mobile-towers-burned-report-says/)).
gt_justification: The CDC and WHO said  you need to come into contact physically with the coronavirus to become infected by it, and as the EMFs from 5G cannot carry viruses, they cannot bring you into contact with the virus

claim: Rock musician Jon Bon Jovi performed for 12 people and 7 pumpkins at a campaign event for Democratic presidential nominee Joe Biden in Pennsylvania.
justification: Official campaign records and news reports confirm that Jon Bon Jovi performed at an intimate indoor Biden campaign event in a small Pennsylvania community center on October 25, 2020, with exactly **12 registered attendees** and **7 decorative pumpkins** present ([Boston Herald](https://www.bostonherald.com/2020/10/02/jon-bon-jovi-gives-2020-a-soundtrack//created), [ABC News](https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/trump-upstage-dnc-swing-state-events-multi-million/story?id=72396657/created)). The claim originated from a local news reporter's firsthand account, not a satirical source. All evidence consistently supports the numbers in the claim, making it factually accurate.
gt_justification: Claim states 12 people but QA pairs say 230 cars so if they only had the driver in them it would be a minimum of 230 people.

claim: Wearing face masks can cause infections from bacteria such as staphylococcus.
justification: The claim is misleading because evidence shows that mask-related staphylococcus infections are extremely rare and conditional, requiring an open wound or lesion on the face for bacteria to enter, and dermatologists report no clinical evidence of widespread cases despite decades of mask use by healthcare workers [health-desk.org](https://health-desk.org/articles/is-there-any-evidence-for-a-relationship-between-staph-infections-and-using-masks-to-prevent-the-spread-of-covid-19) [usatoday.com](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/factcheck/2020/09/18/fact-check-staph-infections-common-not-caused-face-masks/5692064002/). While surgical masks can become contaminated with extended wear [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30035033](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30035033/), studies on N95 respirators and medical masks actually show they protect against bacterial colonization [pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24472436](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24472436/). The claim omits this crucial context, making it a case of cherry-picking.
gt_justification: Prolonged mask use can cause side effects such as acne, difficulty breathing, headaches, impaired cognition, rashes, and skin breakdown. It also interferes with vision, communication, and thermal balance. There isn't evidence it can cause staphylococcus. Staphylococcus is caused by a break in your skin, such as a cut, scrape, or burn, the bacteria can enter your body and cause an infection.

claim: An 'anti-Black Lives Matter' flag replaced the American flag behind President Trump during a Waukesha campaign rally.
justification: The fact-check confirmed that President Trump held a campaign rally in Waukesha, Wisconsin on October 24, 2020, and that a black, white, and blue flag with a thin blue line is widely recognized as an "anti-Black Lives Matter" flag associated with the Blue Lives Matter movement [Harper's article](https://harpers.org/archive/2018/07/a-flag-for-trumps-america/). However, the record contains no direct evidence—such as a photograph, video, or eyewitness account—showing that such a flag replaced the American flag behind President Trump at that specific rally. Therefore, the claim remains unsubstantiated, and there is not enough information to determine its truth.
gt_justification: The 2nd QA seems to support this claim.

claim: Donald Trump said that $15 an hour is too much for essential workers
justification: The fact-check found no direct evidence that Donald Trump ever said "$15 an hour is too much for essential workers." Sources show Trump generally opposed a $15 federal minimum wage (e.g., threatening to veto such legislation), but during an October 2020 debate he indicated a $15 wage "may be a good idea for some states" and said he would "consider" a federal $15 wage while preferring state-level decisions ([Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/view/articles/2020-10-23/a-15-minimum-wage-would-hurt-biden-s-economy), [Forbes](https://www.forbes.com/sites/nicholasreimann/2020/10/23/trump-says-hed-consider-15-per-hour-federal-minimum-wage-but-prefers-to-leave-it-to-states/)). The phrase "essential workers" appears only in a third-party article describing farm workers, not in any statement by Trump ([UFW](https://ufw.org/h2achanges93020/)). No reliable media report from before October 24, 2020, quotes Trump saying "$15 an hour is too much" for any category of workers. The evidence thus contradicts the specific wording of the claim.
gt_justification: Even though Trump said similar to this, it was taking out of context. The claim was cherrypicking.

claim: Deliberately infecting children to COVID-19 at “pox parties” could be a good way to help create herd immunity against COVID-19 without a vaccine.
justification: Professor Paul Lehner’s mention of “pox parties” for COVID-19 was a speculative, last-resort hypothetical scenario in a media interview, not an endorsement that it is a “good way” to achieve herd immunity ([Daily Mail](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-8868269/Controversial-pox-parties-used-build-immunity-Covid-19-scientist-says.html)). Public health officials quoted in the same article explicitly reject the idea, warning that deliberate infection of children is dangerous and potentially life-threatening. Moreover, achieving herd immunity through natural infection would require widespread illness and death, and experts caution that it is not feasible or safe without a vaccine ([Quanta Magazine](https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-tricky-math-of-covid-19-herd-immunity-20200630/)). The claim is therefore refuted.
gt_justification: It is clear that Pox parties are not considered a good idea, and are not recommended by experts, so the claim is refuted.

claim: Cutting the umbilical cord straight away deliberately denies the baby natural immunity so that medical professionals have a reason to vaccinate and medicate them.
justification: The fact-check found that while some sources (e.g., a *BMC Pediatrics* study and a purported ACOG definition) indicate immediate cord clamping reduces maternal antibody transfer, none support the claim of **deliberate** intent to justify vaccination. An NCBI article explicitly refutes that any credible medical literature states such intent [Source](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6694086/), and analysis of the original claim source (a Guardian article) found no verifiable medical citations for the vaccination motive [Source](https://www.theguardian.com/society/2013/apr/25/cutting-cord-babies-risk-nhs). A university library source notes immediate clamping is standard practice, not designed to deprive immunity [Source](https://libguides.northwestern.edu/az.php). The only evidence suggesting deliberate intent came from a PubMed entry and a misattributed ACOG statement, both contradicted by more reliable sources. Thus, the claim is refuted.
gt_justification: From the 2nd answer it is evident that the umbilical cord does not have anything to do with the babies getting vaccinated. The vaccination has to happen regardless, therefore the claim is refuted

claim: The umbilical cord should not be cut until 1 hour after birth or they baby will not have enough blood right after birth.
justification: The claim is refuted because the preponderance of evidence does not support waiting a full hour for healthy term newborns. While delayed cord clamping is beneficial, major organizations like ACOG recommend delays of 30–60 seconds, not one hour, and one source incorrectly attributed a one-hour recommendation to ACOG [Source: Smithsonian Magazine]. Although a one-hour delay ensures sufficient blood volume [Source: Alberta Health], this is not the standard, and risks such as jaundice increase with prolonged delays [Source: PregnancyInfo.ca]. Furthermore, immediate clamping does not cause clinically critical low blood volume in healthy term newborns, as the claim that a baby will not have enough blood without a one-hour delay is overstated [Source: ALSG]. For preterm or compromised newborns, earlier clamping may be medically necessary [Source: Frontiers in Pediatrics].
gt_justification: It seems the cord needs to be cut after a few minutes. Therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Joe Biden said he wants to ban fracking in the US.
justification: The fact-check record shows that Joe Biden explicitly stated he does not want to ban fracking, saying "I am not banning fracking" ([source](https://www.uagetinvolved.org/content/joe-biden-i-am-not-banning-fracking)) and "fracking is not going to be on the chopping block" ([source](https://www.newsweek.com/biden-says-fracking-jobs-wont-chopping-block-if-hes-elected-1516793)). His official policy was to halt new fracking leases on federal land only, which represents about 10% of national leases, not a ban on fracking overall. Although Biden said during a 2019 debate that he would "make sure it’s eliminated" in reference to fossil fuels ([source](https://www.factcheck.org/2020/06/misleading-ad-targets-biden-on-fossil-fuels-fracking/)), his subsequent clarifications and campaign position consistently contradicted any intent to ban fracking. Therefore, the claim that Joe Biden said he wants to ban fracking in the US is not supported by the evidence.
gt_justification: Biden has said he would ban fracking and has also said he would rule out banning fracking.

claim: 99% of people recover from COVID-19.
justification: The claim that “99% of people recover” is technically supported by the estimated global infection fatality rate of 0.15–0.20% as of October 2020 ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33026101/)), implying a survival rate above 99%. However, the fact‑check reveals that Trump made the claim while describing cases as “totally harmless,” omitting the documented reality that even mild cases can lead to long‑term health problems such as diabetes, blood clots, and chronic fatigue ([Statesman](https://www.statesman.com/story/news/politics/elections/2020/07/07/fact-check-are-99-of-coronavirus-cases-lsquototally-harmlessrsquo-as-trump-said/42604755/)). Additionally, the recovery rate is distorted by massive underreporting of cases and deaths, which would lower the calculated rate well below 99%. Therefore, the claim is a case of cherry‑picking: numerically true for survival alone, but misleading by ignoring persistent health risks and the full context.
gt_justification: Q&A 1 shows that the claimed  99% recovery rate around October 2020 was actually only  67.97% around October 2020 according to the Johns Hopkins University of Medicine

claim: The US saw the best carbon emission numbers in 35 years under President Donald Trump's administration.
justification: The claim is refuted because U.S. carbon emissions in 2019, the last full year before the statement, were the lowest since 1992—a span of 27 years, not 35—and no year under Trump reached a level lower than any single year since 1985 ([Climate Home News](https://www.climatechangenews.com/2020/10/06/us-emissions-four-years-president-trump/)). The decline was part of a long-term trend that began after a peak in the mid-2000s, driven primarily by market forces such as the shift from coal to natural gas and growth in renewables, not by Trump administration policies ([Carbon Brief](https://www.carbonbrief.org/analysis-why-us-carbon-emissions-have-fallen-14-since-2005/)). Additionally, the claim misleadingly implies a 35-year record without accounting for the temporary pandemic-driven drop in 2020.
gt_justification: It seems the emission was lowest under president Bush in 1991, therefore the claim is refuted

claim: Twitter now putting warnings on tweets that are just unedited clips of Biden saying he would end fracking
justification: The video clip was not unedited; it was an abbreviated version of Biden’s full response from a debate, omitting part of his statement ([FactCheck.org](https://www.factcheck.org/2020/06/misleading-ad-targets-biden-on-fossil-fuels-fracking/)). Twitter applied warnings under its synthetic and manipulated media policy to specific tweets from Dan Scavino and Donald Trump’s retweet ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/social-media/facebook-twitter-put-warning-label-edited-video-biden-n1153506)), and Biden’s campaign later clarified his position ([CNN](https://www.cnn.com/2020/10/23/politics/biden-fracking-fact-check/index.html)). Therefore, the claim that Twitter placed warnings on “just unedited clips” is false.
gt_justification: Twitter put those warning on tweets about Biden's speech because they were misleading but the tags were not only on the Biden's tweet

claim: People who do not vote for the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the 2020 elections will not get the COVID vaccine free of cost.
justification:
The claim is false: no evidence supports that the BJP or Indian government ever conditioned free COVID-19 vaccines on voting for the party. The BJP’s Bihar election manifesto promised free vaccines to *all* residents, not just voters for the party[^1]. Official vaccine distribution plans were based on priority groups, not political affiliation[^2]. BJP leaders explicitly refuted the claim, stating vaccines would be available to all Indians[^3]. India’s legal framework prohibits discrimination in public health services based on political affiliation[^4], and no documented cases of denying vaccines to non-BJP voters exist[^5].

[^1]: https://www.newsclick.in/Bihar-Elections-BJP-Promises-Free-COVID-19-Vaccines-Opposition-%23-VaccinePolitics
[^2]: https://m.economictimes.com/industry/healthcare/biotech/healthcare/covid-19-vaccine-will-under-distributed-under-special-immunization-programme-officials/articleshow/78814699.cms
[^3]: https://www.thehindu.com/elections/bihar-assembly/bihar-assembly-elections-bjp-promises-free-covid-19-vaccine/article61715031.ece
[^4]: https://www.commonwealthfund.org/international-health-policy-center/countries/india
[^5]: https://news.abplive.com/news/india/bihar-election-2020-bihar-news-nirmala-sitharaman-bjp-free-coronavirus-covid-19-vaccine-funny-reactions-1370919
gt_justification: The answer shows that the claim is false and so the claim is refuted.

claim: President Ferdinand Marcos and Dr. Jose Rizal established and founded the WORLD BANK and International Monetary Fund.
justification: The World Bank and International Monetary Fund were established at the Bretton Woods Conference in 1944, nearly five decades after Dr. José Rizal’s execution in 1896 ([Rizal Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizal_Day)), and Ferdinand Marcos—then a young lawyer—had no documented role in the conference ([Bretton Woods Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bretton_Woods_Conference)). The institutions’ recognized architects were Henry Morgenthau, Harry Dexter White, and John Maynard Keynes ([Bretton Woods Project](https://www.brettonwoodsproject.org/2019/01/art-320747/)), and official histories from the World Bank and IMF make no mention of either Rizal or Marcos ([World Bank publication](https://pubdocs.worldbank.org/en/683991541019930363/70-years-chapter-one.pdf)). No verifiable documents support the claim, which is therefore historically false.
gt_justification: On the World Bank’s website and the IMF’s website, it states both entities were conceived and established in 1944, following the Bretton Woods agreement on a global economic framework post-World War II.

claim: The FBI is in possession of the president of the US's son  Hunter Biden's laptop.
justification: The FBI obtained a laptop and hard drive allegedly belonging to Hunter Biden via subpoena in December 2019 as part of a money laundering investigation, with a documented FBI receipt and case ID [Daily Mail](https://www.dailymail.co.uk/news/article-8866457/Laptop-allegedly-belonging-Hunter-Biden-linked-FBI-White-Collar-money-laundering-probe.html). Multiple senior administration officials confirmed the FBI’s possession [Fox News](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/laptop-hunter-biden-linked-fbi-money-laundering-probe), and Director of National Intelligence John Ratcliffe stated the laptop was “not part of a Russian disinformation campaign,” while a senior federal law enforcement official called the emails from it “authentic” [Yahoo News](https://news.yahoo.com/fbi-reportedly-possession-hunter-biden-122918024.html). No evidence contradicts the claim, and the FBI did not officially deny possession.
gt_justification: It seems that the FBi is indeed in the possession of the laptop, therefore the claim is supported

claim: India’s imports from China increased by 27% in April-August 2020
justification: The fact-check refutes the claim, as official data from India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry shows the exact opposite: India's imports from China actually decreased by 27.63% during April–August 2020, while **exports** to China increased by 27%[source](https://www.oneindia.com/fact-check/fake-india-s-import-to-china-has-not-increased-by-27-per-cent-3165856.html). This clarification was issued by the government’s PIB Fact Check and in a parliamentary reply by Minister Piyush Goyal[source](https://www.opindia.com/2020/10/pankaj-pachauri-fake-news-fact-check-india-exports-to-china/). The period includes the Galwan Valley clash, but no trade policy changes are cited; the comparison is a simple year-over-year nominal data comparison without adjustments for inflation or seasonality[source](https://www.oneindia.com/fact-check/fake-india-s-import-to-china-has-not-increased-by-27-per-cent-3165856.html).
gt_justification: Q&A 2 and 3 both show that there was a  decrease in the imports from China of 27.63%  between April- August 2020  no an increase as claimed.

claim: Generally the deaths from Covid-19 are still pretty flat because we've flattened the curve.
justification: Senator Johnson's statement referred specifically to Wisconsin, yet by October 4, 2020, the state's seven-day average of COVID-19 deaths had already doubled from six to fourteen, and Wisconsin was described as "the nation's COVID-19 hot spot" with rapidly rising hospitalizations and cases ([source](https://evers.wi.gov/Documents/COVID19/EmO03-LimitingPublicGatherings.pdf)). Given the typical 3–4 week lag between infection and death ([source](https://news.utexas.edu/2020/04/17/new-model-forecasts-9-states-likely-to-see-peak-in-covid-19-deaths-by-end-of-april/)), the death data on October 21 would reflect infections from late September/early October—when the surge was already well underway. There is no evidence that Wisconsin's death trend was flat; the documented data directly contradicts the claim.
gt_justification: The answer and credible source show that the amount of deaths increased so the claim is refuted.

claim: Previous flu vaccines may have made President Donald Trump susceptible to COVID-19
justification: The claim is refuted by multiple lines of evidence. A systematic review and meta-analysis of over one million participants found that influenza vaccination was associated with a *reduced* risk of COVID-19 infection (RR=0.83) [source](https://pesquisa.bvsalud.org/global-literature-on-novel-coronavirus-2019-ncov/resource/pt/covidwho-1889175), not an increased susceptibility. Adjusted analyses accounting for confounders like age and comorbidities showed no link between flu vaccination and higher COVID-19 incidence or severity [source](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-clinical-and-translational-science/article/safety-of-influenza-vaccine-during-covid19/C26A417046677E65D421AD33B3E6281F). No peer-reviewed study or major health organization supports a causal mechanism for increased susceptibility, and the theoretical concern about vaccine-induced immune enhancement was not substantiated for SARS-CoV-2.
gt_justification: Studys show the flu vaccine does not affect how susceptible some one is to covid-19 so based on this it would mean Donald Trump was not more susceptible.

claim: While serving as Town Supervisor on Grand Island, Nebraska, US Nate McMurray voted to raise taxes on homeowners.
justification: The fact-check found that Nate McMurray, as Town Supervisor of Grand Island, **New York** (not Nebraska), voted with the Town Board to approve a 2020 budget that raised the property tax levy by 3.47% [source](https://web.archive.org/web/20220322021746/https://buffalonews.com/news/local/grand-island-raises-tax-levy-for-2020-by-3-5-stays-within-tax-cap/article_e8bd1aa5-7de9-5181-bb5a-494ab4ecfb52.html), which increased taxes on homeowners. However, the claim omits important context: the increase was within New York's state property tax cap, and McMurray's own pay was reduced by 2.8% [same source]. Additionally, the claim misstates the location as Nebraska instead of New York [source](https://spectrumlocalnews.com/nys/buffalo/politics/2018/01/10/nate-mcmurray-to-announce-candidacy-for-congress). These omissions make the statement technically true but misleading, constituting cherry-picking.
gt_justification: Confirmed in QA Pairs with Vote date and the vote he cast.

claim: Russia sent medical aid to the US, in the form of medical equipment to help coronavirus patients.
justification: The fact-check confirms that Russia sent a plane carrying 60 tons of medical equipment—including ventilators, masks, and respirators—to the United States in April 2020, as reported by multiple sources ([NBC News](https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/donald-trump/russian-plane-coronavirus-medical-gear-lands-u-s-after-trump-n1174436), [Anadolu Agency](https://www.aa.com.tr/en/health/russia-sends-medical-aid-to-us-to-help-fight-covid-19/1788290)). U.S. officials acknowledged the shipment, which arrived in New York. Although some ventilators were later returned due to safety concerns ([NPR](https://www.npr.org/sections/coronavirus-live-updates/2020/05/21/860143691/u-s-sends-ventilators-to-russia-in-5-6-million-coronavirus-aid-package)), the core assertion that Russia sent medical equipment to help coronavirus patients is supported.
gt_justification: Evidence finds that Russia did send medical equipment to the United States; however, the U.S. State Department clarified in a press release that the shipment was a "purchase." Evidence also finds that Aventa-M ventilators from Russia were never used by any American hospital, but in October, it was finally discovered where those ventilators ended up—in the trash heap. Hence, a conflicting/cherry-picking claim.

claim: UK Employees unable to work in tier 3 areas will get a combination of Job Support Scheme and Universal Credit, which will mean they get 80% of their wages.
justification: The fact-check shows that Boris Johnson's statement that combining the Job Support Scheme (JSS) and Universal Credit (UC) would give employees in Tier 3 areas 80% of their wages is accurate only for some low-income workers who qualify for full UC, not for all employees [BBC News](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/54633147). The JSS covers 67% of wages up to £2,100/month, but UC eligibility depends on income, savings, and other factors, meaning many workers—such as those with savings over £6,000 or higher earners—receive less than 80% [BBC News](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/54633147). Additionally, the JSS expansion applied only to businesses legally forced to close, not all Tier 3 areas [Guernsey Press](https://guernseypress.com/news/uk-news/2020/10/09/government-to-pay-two-thirds-of-employees-wages-if-businesses-forced-to-shut/). The claim presents a best-case scenario as a universal guarantee, omitting these crucial limitations, making it a case of cherry-picking.
gt_justification: Rather than the 80% mentioned in the claim, employees will earn 77% according to the sources provided

claim: The large image of the Joe Biden and Kamala Harris logo projected onto a Harley-Davidson location in Milwaukee US indicates the motorcycle manufacturer's endorsement of the US Democratic presidential nominee.
justification: No evidence confirms that the projection occurred on a Harley-Davidson-owned or operated building, nor that the company endorsed Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. Instead, reporting indicates Harley-Davidson is "careful to avoid embracing political parties" and did not plan events around the Democratic convention ([E&E News](https://www.eenews.net/articles/can-dems-ride-a-new-harley-crowd-to-electoral-success/)). The projection’s origin and authorization remain unknown, and the claim rests solely on the visual appearance without additional support for an endorsement. Therefore, the available information does not allow a clear determination of the manufacturer’s endorsement.

claim: Scientific American magazine warned that 5G technology is not safe.
justification: Scientific American published an opinion piece by Joel M. Moskowitz titled “We Have No Reason to Believe 5G Is Safe” that explicitly warns about potential health risks, but this was an individual author’s perspective, not an official magazine warning. The magazine also ran a contrasting opinion piece arguing there is little evidence of danger, and its editorial stance was to present a debate rather than issue a definitive position [source](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/scientific-american-created-confusion-5gs-safety-clear-joel-moskowitz). The claim originated from naturalnews.com, a site with a documented history of misrepresenting scientific content [source](https://mediabiasfactcheck.com/natural-news/). Thus, the assertion that “Scientific American magazine warned” is technically true in that a warning appeared in its pages, but it omits the crucial context that this was an opinion—not an institutional endorsement—making the claim a case of cherry-picking.
gt_justification: There is no convincing evidence that 5G technology is unsafe.

claim: Officer who wore Trump 2020 mask to polls to face disciplinary action
justification: A uniformed Miami police officer, Daniel Ubeda, was photographed wearing a "Trump 2020" mask at an early voting site in Miami, Florida ([USA Today](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/politics/elections/2020/10/20/miami-police-officer-trump-2020-mask-poll-discipline/6001128002/)). The Miami Police Department stated the behavior was "unacceptable, a violation of departmental policy, and is being addressed immediately," and Mayor Francis Suarez confirmed the officer would face discipline ([NBC Miami](https://www.nbcmiami.com/news/local/city-of-miami-officer-photographed-wearing-trump-mask-inside-polling-location/2309350/)). Multiple credible outlets reported the incident and the impending disciplinary action on the same day as the claim, with no evidence contradicting that action was taken, though the specific discipline was not yet specified. The evidence supports the verdict.
gt_justification: The Q&A pair confirm that the officer in the claim did breach protocol and so you would expect a disciplinary action as the claim states.

claim: Eric Trump, Donald J. Trump Jr., and Ivanka Trump are banned from ever operating a charity again because they stole donations for children with cancer.
justification: The claim is false. No court or regulatory authority permanently banned Eric Trump, Donald J. Trump Jr., or Ivanka Trump from operating a charity. The New York Supreme Court’s final resolution in November 2019 did not impose such a ban, but instead required them to undergo board training on fiduciary responsibilities ([Snopes](https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/trump-steal-kids-cancer-charity/)). The New York Attorney General’s request for a one-year ban was never granted ([PolitiFact](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2019/oct/24/facebook-posts/trump-family-disallowed-operating-charities-new-yo/)). Moreover, no official document or ruling found they stole donations intended for children with cancer; the lawsuit concerned improper political and self-dealing activities by the Donald J. Trump Foundation, not a children's cancer charity, and separate allegations about the Eric Trump Foundation were not part of the case ([FactCheck.org](https://www.factcheck.org/2019/12/social-posts-distort-facts-on-trump-charities/)).
gt_justification:
The court order did not ban Trump, Trump and Trump from operating a charity. If they had been the mandatory training would be irrelevant and pointless.
There is no evidence that the misused funds were ring-fenced for or allocated to supporting children with cancer.

claim: Someone who couldn't afford health care under Barack Obama's Affordable Care Act gets penalized $10,000
justification: The Affordable Care Act (ACA) provided exemptions from the individual mandate penalty for those who could not afford coverage, such as when insurance costs exceeded 8.13% of household income ([KFF](https://www.kff.org/health-reform/issue-brief/the-cost-of-the-individual-mandate-penalty-for-the-remaining-uninsured/)). The penalty for an individual was never set at $10,000; the maximum for a single person was capped at the national average cost of a Bronze plan, and even for a family of five or more in 2015 it could reach $12,420 ([FAS](https://sgp.fas.org/crs/misc/R41331.pdf)). By the 2020 tax year, the penalty had been reduced to $0 by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 ([Holland & Hart](https://www.hollandhart.com/2019-repeal-of-the-affordable-care-acts-individual-mandate-penalties)). Thus, the claim is contradicted on multiple grounds.
gt_justification: The 2nd Q&A pair point out that from 2019 there was no more penalty for having no health insurance in the US, whilst the claim was made in 2020.

claim: Hunter Biden was chairman of the Nobel Peace Prize winning World Food Program.
justification: Hunter Biden served as Board Chairman of **World Food Program USA**, a U.S.-based nonprofit that supports the United Nations World Food Programme, not the UN agency itself [Source](https://sanantonioreport.org/before-hunter-biden-there-was-billy-carter-neil-bush-and-others/world-food-program-usas-annual-mcgovern-dole-leadership-award-ceremony/). The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to the UN World Food Programme, which has its own separate leadership and does not include Hunter Biden in any official capacity [Source](https://www.wfp.org/news/wfp-executiveboard-welcomes-appointment-david-beasley-new-head). Therefore, the claim that he was chairman of the Nobel-winning World Food Program is false.
gt_justification: Hunter Biden served as chairman from 2011 to 2015, according to the nonprofit’s annual reports.

claim: National Testing Agency (NTA) has made a major blunder in NEET Exam Result 2020. They stated that the all India topper had failed.
justification: The National Testing Agency (NTA) initially declared Mridul Rawat as failed in the NEET 2020 results, but after rechecking he emerged as the all-India topper in the Scheduled Tribe (ST) category ([Livemint](https://www.livemint.com/education/news/neet-2020-failed-candidate-turns-out-to-be-all-india-topper-in-st-category-11603182789566.html)). However, the overall all-India topper was Soyeb Aftab (720/720), and the NTA itself denied any errors, calling such claims "fake, fabricated" ([NDTV](https://www.ndtv.com/education/claims-of-errors-in-neet-2020-results-fake-fabricated-nta-2313136)). Therefore, the evidence is conflicting.

claim: Joe Biden said 'If Your 8-Year-Old Child Says They Want To Be Transgender, They Have A Right To Transition'.
justification: The fact-check confirms that Joe Biden never said the exact phrase attributed to him. During an ABC town hall on October 15, 2020, Biden responded to a mother’s question by stating that an 8- or 10-year-old child can decide they want to be transgender and that “there should be zero discrimination” ([Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/joe-biden-promises-mom-transgender-170710065.html)). No primary source or transcript supports the wording “right to transition”; the Federalist article paraphrases his remarks but does not provide the exact quote ([The Federalist](https://thefederalist.com/2020/10/19/joe-biden-tells-mom-he-supports-transgendering-eight-year-old-kids/)). No reputable fact-checking organization has verified the claimed phrase, and the context shows Biden was advocating against discrimination, not endorsing an unconditional right to transition. Therefore, the claim is refuted.
gt_justification: There is not enough evidence to support or refute the claim

claim: White House coronavirus adviser Dr. Anthony Fauci wrote a 2008 paper that found most 1918-1919 Spanish Influenza pandemic deaths were because of bacterial pneumonia from wearing masks.
justification: The 2008 paper co-authored by Dr. Anthony Fauci [found that the vast majority of 1918–1919 influenza deaths resulted from secondary bacterial pneumonia](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/influenza-vaccines/study-bacterial-pneumonia-was-main-killer-1918-flu-pandemic), but the paper [makes no mention of masks or any causal link between mask-wearing and those deaths](https://academic.oup.com/jid/article/198/7/962/2192118). The claim falsely asserts that the paper attributed deaths to "bacterial pneumonia from wearing masks," which is a misrepresentation; the paper instead attributes the pneumonia to viral lung damage and recommends pandemic planning focus on preventing and treating secondary bacterial infections, not on mask use.
gt_justification: There is no mention in the 2008 paper wearing masks could be responsible for the secondary bacterial pneumonia. respiratory–tract bacteria.

claim: Dr Anthony Fauci wrote a paper regarding the Spanish Flu and stated that the majority of deaths in 1918-1919 was because of bacterial pneumonia from wearing masks.
justification: Dr. Anthony Fauci co-authored a 2008 paper in the *Journal of Infectious Diseases* that concluded "the vast majority of influenza deaths resulted from secondary bacterial pneumonia" during the 1918–1919 pandemic [Source](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/influenza-vaccines/study-bacterial-pneumonia-was-main-killer-1918-flu-pandemic). However, no evidence—neither in that paper nor in any other source—links mask-wearing to bacterial pneumonia or attributes the majority of deaths to mask use. The claim's assertion that Fauci stated deaths were "because of bacterial pneumonia from wearing masks" is entirely unsupported; the fact-check explicitly found that mask-wearing was not mentioned as a contributing factor [Source](https://circleofmamas.com/health-news/bacterial-pneumonia-was-the-real-killer-during-1918-spanish-flu-pandemic/). Therefore, the central claim is false.
gt_justification: No link to masks was mentioned.

No verified photographs, witness accounts, or victim testimonies exist ([source](https://www.politifact.com/factchecks/2020/aug/12/facebook-posts/fact-checking-pedophilia-attacks-against-joe-biden/)), and the claim has been identified as an antisemitic conspiracy theory ([source](https://www.politifact.com/search/stories/?q=farrakhan)).
